Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-02
November 19, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting - FOR ACTION
(Introduced at the September 17, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting)
Extends deadline for course withdrawals without extenuating circumstances
Approved by FSEC 10/28/26 (as amended)
Legislation effective starting Fall 2027
Rationale: URI’s current policy for course withdrawals allows students to withdraw from a course by week six into the semester. At the end of week six, they need to have extenuating circumstances with supporting documentation for approval of a late drop. Many - most - courses do not post midterm grades by week six, however, making students predict their success in the course before they have any real data. Students either drop the course for fear of not doing well and miss the chance to succeed or stay in and try and succeed when they should have dropped it. When students ask for a W too late, without extenuating circumstances, their late drop petition gets denied even if their reasoning is sound.

For regular session classes, the revised version of this legislation would extend the “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” deadline for undergraduate students from six weeks to nine weeks. Graduate students would continue to have the existing deadline of six weeks.
This original version of this legislation was introduced for discussion at the 9/17/26 Faculty Senate meeting. The final version has been revised as follows in response to faculty/staff comments.
1. Moved the “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” deadline from 11 weeks (originally proposed) to nine weeks. Although five of the ten comparable institutions surveyed (see below) have “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” deadlines at 11 weeks, there was concern about making such a substantial change.

2. Maintained the current ‘Drop through Ecampus’ option for students between the fourth and sixth weeks in the regular semester. The original legislation eliminated the ability of students to drop classes through Ecampus after the three-week add period. The revised legislation does not change the existing ‘Drop through Ecampus’ option for weeks 4-6. As a result, there should be minimal/no change in the total number of withdrawal forms processed.
3. Removed faculty signatures on “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” forms submitted between the sixth and ninth weeks. Faculty signatures are currently required for withdrawals after the sixth week of classes. To reduce administrative burden, faculty signatures would no longer be required for withdrawals occurring before the end of the ninth week. As per current practice, faculty signatures would still be required for withdrawal requests submitted after the ninth week of classes.

4. Restricted the legislation to undergraduate students. The current withdrawal policy applies to both graduate and undergraduate students. The Graduate School has requested that graduate students retain the six-week ‘withdraw without extenuating circumstances’ deadline.
DATA
Ten comparable universities were reviewed: half allow late drops without extenuating circumstances until the eleventh week of the regular semester, and all have a later date than URI and the same withdrawal date for graduate and undergraduate students.
*See “Addendum to Proposal Change to URI’s Late Withdrawal of a Course Policy” document to review the comparable universities and their full policies

Potential impacts: This proposal has been vetted by ESAC (Enrollment Services Advisory Committee), a URI internal administrative body that includes academic deans or representatives from each degree-granting college and the directors of student-supporting service offices. To ensure that undergraduate students understand the academic and/or financial implications of a ‘W’, ESAC recommended that course withdrawal forms remain required between the end of the six-week ‘Drop in ECampus’ period and the last day of classes. Each form must be signed by an academic affairs advisor/dean of the college in which the student is enrolled before being processed by enrollment services.
This proposal should not change the number of withdrawal forms being processed, and the per-form processing time for undergraduate withdrawal forms submitted between weeks 6-9 will be reduced significantly because students no longer need to provide extenuating circumstances. There will be fewer meetings and less work required for undergraduate students to document extenuating circumstances.

This change will also greatly benefit staff working in areas such as Health Services, Student Support & Advocacy Services, and Disability, Access, & Inclusion. Over the past four Fall semesters (see below), an average of 1,379 “Withdraw with extenuating circumstances” requests were processed each semester. Each of these requests required someone at the university to certify them as such, a process that takes a substantial amount of time each semester. The new policy would reduce the average number of “Withdraw with extenuating circumstances” requests from 1,379 to 847 per semester, a ~40% decrease.

ORIGINAL 8.34.10 Dropping a Course. A course may be dropped by official procedures determined by the Office of Enrollment Services (e-campus) on or before the end of the third week of classes (Drop Period) with no mark on a student’s transcript. Courses may be dropped through e-campus between the fourth and the end of the sixth week of classes (Withdrawal Period) and will be recognized on a student’s transcript with a “W.” After the end of the sixth week (Late Withdrawal Period), a student may drop a course only in exceptional circumstances and only with authorization of the dean of the college in which the student is enrolled. Such drops will also be recognized on a student’s transcript with a “W.” If the student has not dropped a course by the end of the withdrawal period the instructor must submit a grade. All requests to drop courses after the end of the Late Withdrawal Period must be requested/approved by the student’s academic dean by the last day of classes for the term in which the drop is sought. Only in exceptional circumstances and with significant supporting documentation will exceptions to this deadline be considered. Failure or low grades on assignments/exams or lack of attendance do not constitute exceptional circumstances. Fees will not be adjusted downward for courses dropped after the end of the “add” period (see 8.43.20 for adjustment of fees). #10-11—23, #12-13–24, #21-22-6

PROPOSED 8.34.10 Dropping a Course.
A regular session course may be dropped by official procedures determined by the Office of Enrollment Services (e-campus) on or before the end of the third week of classes (Drop Period) with no mark on a student’s transcript.
Courses may be dropped through e-campus between the fourth and the end of the sixth week of classes (Withdrawal Period) and will be recognized on a student’s transcript with a “W.” Undergraduate students may drop between the end of the sixth week and the end of the ninth week (Withdrawal Period) with authorization of the dean of the college in which the student is enrolled and will be recognized on a student’s transcript with a “W.” After the end of the sixth ninth week (Late Withdrawal Period), undergraduate students may drop a course only in exceptional circumstances and only with authorization of the dean of the college in which the student is enrolled.
Such drops will also be recognized on a student’s transcript with a “W.” If the student has not dropped a course by the end of the withdrawal period the instructor must submit a grade.

Graduate students wishing to drop a course after the end of the sixth week of classes may do so only in exceptional circumstances and only with authorization of the dean of the college in which the student is enrolled.
All requests to drop courses after the end of the Late Withdrawal Period must be requested/approved by the student’s academic dean by the last day of classes for the term in which the drop is sought.
Only in exceptional circumstances and with significant supporting documentation will exceptions to this deadline be considered.
Failure or low grades on assignments/exams or lack of attendance do not constitute exceptional circumstances.
Fees will not be adjusted downward for courses dropped after the end of the “add” period (see 8.43.20 for adjustment of fees). #10-11—23, #12-13–24, #21-22-6

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-03 November 19, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting Creation of a College Liaison Special Committee (one semester trial) Approved by FSEC 11/04/26 Effective Date: Start of spring semester 2027 The College Liaison Special Committee (CLSC) shall consist of up to ten senators, one from each college that elects Faculty Senators and one from the Library (henceforth referred to as ‘units’) , who are referred to as the ‘Liaison’ from their unit to the Faculty Senate.
If the Faculty Senate votes to approve creation of this Special Committee in fall 2026 , Senate Staff will contact senators from each unit and solicit volunteer(s) from among their number to serve as the Liaison from that unit during the spring 2027 semester .
If there are multiple volunteers from a given unit, senators from that unit will vote to elect one liaison from among their senators volunteering for the role.
CLSC membership will be confirmed by Faculty Senate vote prior to its beginning work.
The CLSC will be chaired by the Vice President of the Faculty Senate, who serves as a non-voting member.

CLSC members are charged with ensuring that faculty in each college are informed of pertinent university-level matters and communicate senate- and college-level concerns in both directions.
Liaisons attend all-college faculty meetings and will be given the opportunity to give a report on senate activities.
Liaisons also attend meetings of the Faculty Senate in their role as a current senator.
Liaisons will have two responsibilities in addition to attending college- and senate-level meetings.
First, Liaisons provide a monthly written update regarding senate/university-level matters to faculty in their college.
Second, Liaisons represent their college at meetings of the CLSC.
The committee will meet at least once per semester to address issues requiring inter-college coordination.
These may include, but are not limited to, best practices in college-level faculty governance and fostering inter-college research or academic collaborations.
Liaisons are encouraged to submit topics for discussion at CLSC meetings to the Faculty Senate Vice President, who will compile them into a meeting agenda.

The CLSC can vote to refer a matter to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for additional consideration and possible action by the full Senate.
At the end of the spring 2027 semester, the Senate Vice President will give a report to the Faculty Senate listing all matters referred by the CLSC during the previous semester and their current status.
At that time, the CLSC may choose to submit legislation requesting Faculty Senate authorization to continue as a Special Committee in the 2027-28 academic year.
If the CLSC does not receive an affirmative reauthorization vote from the Faculty Senate in spring 2027, it shall be dissolved.

Research topics may span areas such as drug discovery, pharmacology, toxicology, pharmaceutics, pharmacokinetics, environmental health, and natural products.
Through structured presentations and discussion, students develop skills in scientific communication, data interpretation, and critical evaluation of research.
Exposes participants to diverse research approaches within pharmaceutical sciences, helping students connect laboratory research with concepts

learned in the classroom.

FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION November 19, 2026 Graduate Council Report 2026-2027-3A At the November 9, 2026 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate COURSE CHANGES COLLEGE OF EDUCATION EDC 586 | Problems in Education, Effective Spring 2027 Change description, repeat criteria, add modality (1-3 crs.) Advanced work for graduate students in education.
Courses conducted as seminars or as supervised individual projects.

Topics include: 'Consortium on Reading Excellence,' 'Hosting a SALT visit,' 'Instructional Strategies for Diversiﬁed Classrooms,' 'Orton-Gillingham Reading Instruction,' 'Orton, Gillingham Reading Practicum,' 'Reﬂective Practitioner-Using Data to Inform Instruction,' 'SALT visit,' 'Schools Attuned,' 'Using Blogs & Wikis to Facilitate Learning,' '4 Roles of Leadership,' 'Using the Internet for Teaching, Learning, & Practical Applications,' 'Seven Habits of Highly Effective People,' 'Teaching the 'Write Traits',' 'Thinking Math II,' and 'Building Teams & Leading Change.' (Independent Study/Accelerated Online Program) Pre: permission of instructor.
May be repeated under different topics a maximum of 5 times.
EDC 587 | Problems in Education, Effective Spring 2027 Change description, repeat criteria, add modality (1-3 crs.) Advanced work for graduate students in education.
Courses conducted as seminars or as supervised individual projects.
Topics include: 'Disciplinary Literacy.' (Independent Study/Accelerated Online Program) Pre: permission of instructor.
May be repeated a maximum of 5 times.

EDC 599 | Master's Thesis Research, Effective Spring 2027 Change description, repeat criteria, add modality (1-3 crs.) Number of credits is determined each semester in consultation with the major professor or program committee. (Independent Study/Accelerated Online Program) S/U credit.
May be repeated for a maximum of 12 credits.

EDP 641 | Scholarly Research and Writing Seminar in Education, Effective Summer 2027 Change title, description, credits, add modality (3 cr.) Advanced post-comprehensive examination and post-dissertation proposal seminar supporting doctoral students’ sustained scholarly writing and dissertation research.
Students develop substantial academic writing projects, such as dissertation chapters, article manuscripts, analytic or methodological memos, or related scholarly genres.
Emphasis is placed on sustainable writing practices, revision, research and argument development, ethical peer feedback, and participation in scholarly communities.
Students also explore professional genres beyond the dissertation, including publication, peer review, public scholarship, grant writing, job materials, and advising feedback. (Seminar/Online) Pre: admission to Ph.D. in Education and successful completion of comprehensive examination May be repeated for a maximum of 6 credits.

EDP 692 | Directed Readings and Research Problems, Effective Spring 2027 Change description, add modality (3-6 crs.) Directed readings and advanced research work under the supervision of a member of the graduate faculty, arranged to suit the individual requirements of the students. (Independent Study/Accelerated Online Program) Pre: permission of instructor.
May be repeated for a maximum of 12 credits.
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES CMD 550 | Audiology for the Speech-Language Pathologist, Effective Summer 2027 Change title, description, remove modality (2 crs.) Introduction to audiology for the speech-language pathology graduate student.
Covers hearing disorders, hearing assessment, child and adult aural rehabilitation. (Lec./Online) Pre: CMD graduate student standing or permission of instructor.
GRADUATE SCHOOL OF OCEANOGRAPHY OCG 548 | Paleoceanography, Effective Fall 2028 Change course number (from OCG 648) (3 crs.) Earth history and its relation to global climate.
Tools, data, and concepts related to past climate change as observed in the oceanic, ice, and terrestrial records. (Lec. 3) Pre: None.

NEW COURSES COLLEGE OF ARTS AND SCIENCES CSC 555 | Large Language Models, Effective Spring 2027 (4 crs.) This course presents Transformer-based architectures and concepts in Large Language Models for training, deployment and research. (Lec. 4) Pre: Permission of the instructor COLLEGE OF BUSINESS BAI 454 | Working with Messy Data, Effective Spring 2027 (3 crs.) This course introduces Python programming as a practical tool for business analytics and data-driven decision-making.
Students learn how to work with real-world business data using Python to clean, transform, visualize, and analyze structured and unstructured text-based datasets.
Emphasis is placed on extracting meaningful insights, communicating results clearly, and translating analytics into actionable managerial recommendations through hands-on projects using Python notebook–based platforms. (Lec. 3) Pre: One of the following: BAI405, CSC201, STA307, SAT308, STA409, BAI311 (previously BAI211)

COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND LIFE SCIENCES NRS 510 | Fundamentals of GIS, Effective Fall 2027 (3 crs.) Applications in using a geographic information system (GIS) to solve spatial problems. Emphasis on ﬁnding existing geospatial datasets; creating new datasets through on-screen digitizing; analyzing spatial data; and presenting data using static maps, interactive web maps, and Story Maps. (Online)

Land Acknowledgment Statement and Student Presentation - Senator Van Wyk and Liliana Mars (matriculating student) - The Land Acknowledgment statement was read into the record and Ms.

Mars noted three upcoming cultural gatherings that the community is welcome to attend.
The first is the Wampanoag Powwow on October 17 in South Dartmouth, which is an educational event highlighting Native practices, history and arts.
The second event is a Lunch and Learn at the Tomaquag Museum being led by URI alum Rene Rico, titled "Reclaiming Healing: Mental Health Care and Resistance to Generational Trauma in Indigenous Communities." Finally, the 51st annual Tarzan Brown Mystic River Run will be held 11/7/26 in Mystic, CT.
The road race honors Ellison Myers "Tarzan" Brown, a Narragansett tribal hero, two-time Boston Marathon winner, and US Olympian.
All are welcome to attend and/or participate. 3.

Status of anonymous concerns submitted to the Faculty Senate - Senate President Preisser announced that this will now be a standing item on meeting agendas to allow the Executive Committee an opportunity to provide answers to questions asked anonymously.
The inaugural inquiry was: Does the university provide guidance as to how long faculty shall hold on to paper tests and quizzes?

Is it in the university manual?
The answer lies in University Manual, §8.52.21: “All papers, exams, reports, etc., submitted by students in fulfillment of course requirements and not returned to students shall be retained by instructors for at least two semesters (not including Summer Session) after the end of the semester in which the items were submitted.” 5 .

Announcements - President Parlange offered brief updates on a number of recent and upcoming events across campus, like the 11th Annual Guitar and Mandolin Festival and the Honors Colloquium.
